courses.repertoire: Giuoco Pianissimo: c3, d3, and a slow build-up
courses.summary: Build with c3 and d3, castle, bring the queen's knight to g3, and break with d4 when ready.
overview: One plan against almost everything: c3 and d3, castle, Re1 and h3, and the knight route b1-d2-f1-g3. Play d4 only when it gains something.
Black's third move decides the chapter: 3...Bc5 comes up in about 40% of your games, and 3...Nf6 in about 30%.
Against 3...Nf6, play 4.d3, not 4.Ng5 or 4.Nc3: e4 stays protected, and you skip the Fried Liver theory and the fork trick.
Keep the Italian bishop. Drop it back to b3 or c2 before ...Na5 or ...b5 can trade it off.
The pin ...Bg4 is harmless here: ask the bishop with h3, guard f3 with Nbd2, and chase it with Ng3 and Nh4.
f7 is Black's weak point. If Black shuts in the f8 bishop with ...d6 and then plays ...Nf6, Ng5 hits f7 at once.

courses.summary: Mirror White's slow setup, keep the bishop with ...a6 and ...Ba7, and know how to meet d4 and the Evans Gambit.
overview: Play 3...Bc5, then ...Nf6, ...d6, ...a6 and ...Ba7. On a7 the bishop survives d4 and b4 and still aims at f2.
In more than half of your games White builds slowly with c3 and d3, or castles first. Mirror the setup: castle, ...h6 to keep White's pieces off g5, ...Re8, then ...Be6 and ...d5.
Don't rush ...d5. Played before you've developed, it lets White's queen join the bishop against d5 and f7 with Qb3.
Against the Center attack (4.c3 and 5.d4), take on d4, check on b4, and free your game with ...d5.
The Møller Attack, 7.Nc3, comes up often: take on e4, because the pin on c3 makes it safe.
Against the Evans Gambit (4.b4), take the pawn, retreat to a5, and give it back with ...d5 at the right moment.

courses.repertoire: One repertoire for both sides: nine Basic lines, plus traps and rarer lines.
courses.summary: 1.e4 c6: the c-pawn supports ...d5, which attacks e4.

why.text:
As Black, you get a solid position with no weak pawns, so trades suit you. Unlike in the French, your light-squared bishop gets out before ...e6.

As White, you meet the Caro-Kann in about 9% of your 1.e4 games. You can choose the kind of game you want, from a space advantage to sharp sidelines full of traps.

rows: White develops quietly: Nf3, Be2 and castling before anything sharp. Black answers ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6, then brings a knight to f5.
White trades the light-squared bishops at once. Black then plays ...e6, ...c5 and ...Nc6, and ...Qb6 also hits b2.
Black plays ...c5 before developing the bishop. After c3 and ...cxd4, ...Bg4 pins the knight that guards d4.
White plays c4 and, after the trades on d5, keeps an isolated d-pawn. Black develops with ...Nf6, ...Nc6 and ...Bg4.
4...Bf5 develops the bishop at once and lets White chase it with Ng3. Club players then often play Nf3, Bd3 and a bishop trade instead of the sharp h4.
Black accepts doubled f-pawns for quick development: ...Bd6, castling and ...Bg4.
White develops before playing d4. With the queen on e2 and a bishop on c4, White sets traps on e7 and f7.
After 4.fxe4 White has two center pawns but a weaker king. Black hits back with ...e5 at once.
Black keeps the center closed and pins the c3 knight with ...Bb4. White answers with a3 and Bd3.
table.note: Share: of all Caro-Kann games (after 1.e4 c6), the share that reach the variation (3.e5, 3...cxd5, 4.Nxe4, 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 or 3.f3), by any move order. At its branch: how often the line's own move is chosen where it branches off. Source: Lichess rated rapid and classical games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. The Maróczy (Fantasy) is rarer, but it is in Basic by choice. Everything else, such as the Exchange with 4.Bd3 or 4.Nf3, the Tal Variation and the Karpov Variation, is in the Advanced section.

courses.repertoire: Advance (3.e5), with 6.a3 in the main line
courses.summary: Gain space with 3.e5, hold d4 with c3 and Nf3, and expand on the queenside with a3 and b4. The Milner-Barry Gambit is a trap-filled surprise weapon.
overview: Play 3.e5. The pawn takes f6 away from Black's king's knight and gives you space; Black answers 3...c5 in nine games out of ten.
Hold d4 with c3 and Nf3. Black's whole plan is pressure on that pawn with ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and a knight on f5.
The main line, 5...Qb6, comes up in a quarter of your games. Play 6.a3 and b4 to gain space; after 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, Nc3 and Na4 chase the queen.
Count the attackers before Black takes on d4. With your queen behind the pawn, ...Nxd4 just drops a piece; with your bishop on d3 in the way, Bb5+ wins Black's queen.
Against 5...Bd7, play 6.Be2 and castle. Avoid 6.Bb5?, which runs into ...Nxe5.
Surprise weapon: the Milner-Barry Gambit, 6.Bd3. It is risky against best play, but Black often grabs too much: 7...Nxd4?? loses the queen, and 10...Qxe5 11.Re1 sets more traps.

courses.repertoire: 3...c5 against the Advance, the Rubinstein (3...dxe4), and ...Nc6 in the Exchange
courses.summary: Build the ...e6 and ...d5 center, attack d4 against the Advance, take on e4 against 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2, and develop actively in the Exchange.
overview: The French idea: ...e6 and ...d5 build a solid center and keep f7 safe. The price is the c8 bishop behind your pawn on e6, so plan to free it or trade it.
The Exchange is your most common opponent, about three games in ten, because 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 exd5 4.d4 leads there too. Develop with ...Nc6, ...Bd6, ...Bg4, ...Qd7 and ...Nge7, and castle short.
Against the Advance (3.e5), about one game in five, hit d4 at once with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6. Against 6.a3, lock the queenside with 6...c4.
Against 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2, take on e4 (the Rubinstein): ...Nd7, ...Ngf6, then ...c5 to free your game.
In the Milner-Barry Gambit (6.Bd3), play ...Bd7 before ...Nxd4. Otherwise 8.Nxd4 Qxd4 9.Bb5+ wins your queen.
Against the Monte Carlo (4.c4), check with 4...Bb4+, castle, and take on c4 only after White's bishop has moved.

courses.repertoire: As White: the Exchange Variation and the minority attack. As Black: the Tartakower Variation.
courses.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6: Black declines the pawn and holds d5 with the e-pawn.

why.text:
As Black, 2...e6 holds the center with a pawn and keeps the position solid. The cost is the c8 bishop, shut in behind e6, so Black's plans are about freeing it.

As White, taking on d5 early fixes the pawn structure. You know your plans in advance, and there are few early tactics to calculate.

rows: Play Bg5, e3, Bd3 and Qc2, and castle. Then the minority attack (Rb1, b4, b5), or Nge2, f3 and e4.
Play ...Be7 and castle. Against 5.Bf4, hit the center with ...c5. Against 5.Bg5, play ...h6 and the Tartakower.
The Tartakower: ...Be7, castle, ...h6, then ...b6 and ...Bb7. If White takes on f6, take back with the bishop.
5.e4 gains time on the knight and builds a full center.
Take on d5 anyway. With no knight on f6 to pin, the bishop goes to f4.
Play 5...Nbd7, which sets the Elephant trap. Then ...c6, ...Be7, castle, ...Re8 and ...Nf8.

courses.repertoire: As White: 3.Nf3 and 4.Nc3, then cxd5 and Bg5 against ...e6. As Black: the Czech Variation (4...dxc4 5.a4 Bf5).
courses.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6: Black guards d5 with the c-pawn.

why.text:
As Black, ...c6 guards d5 and keeps the c8 bishop's diagonal open, so the bishop can come out before ...e6 shuts it in. Solid, with a few exact lines to know.

As White, the Slav often turns into positions you know from the Declined, so the same plans work.

rows: Take on d5, then Bg5, Bd3, Qc2, castle and the minority attack, as in the Exchange Variation.
Take on c4. Against 5.a4, play the Czech Variation: ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bb4 and castle. Against 5.e4 or 5.e3, keep the pawn with 5...b5.
Take on d5 and play Qb3, which hits b7. ...b6? and ...Qd7? lose material.
Copy White's setup: ...Nf6, ...Nc6, ...Bf5 and ...e6. Watch for Qb3 hitting b7.
Play ...Bf5 at once, then ...e6, ...Nbd7 and ...Be7, and castle.
Take on c4 and hold the pawn with ...b5. After 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.e4 b5, 6.a4? loses material to 6...b4!

courses.repertoire: As White: 3.e3 and Bxc4. As Black: ...e5 at once, and the Classical setup against 3.Nf3.
courses.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4: Black takes the pawn and gives up the center for a moment.

why.text:
As Black, giving up the center for a moment frees your pieces, and you get to hit back at White's center early. White wins the pawn back, but you develop quickly.

As White, you win the pawn back at once and keep the center, with a small, safe edge.

rows: Against 4.d5, play ...Nf6. After 5.e4, 5...b5! keeps the extra pawn. Never play ...Bb4 while Qa4+ is possible.
After 4.Bxc4 exd4 5.exd4, White has an isolated pawn: play ...Nf6, ...Bd6 and castle, then ...Nc6 and ...Bg4.
Against 4.d5, play ...Nf6 and ...b5, as against 3.Nc3. Against 4.Nf3, take on d4, then ...Nc6 and ...Be6.
4.Bxc4 and castle. Then trade queens for a small endgame edge, or keep them and push e4.
4.a4 hits the pawn chain. After 4...c6 5.axb5 cxb5, 6.Qf3 wins a piece.
After 4.Bxc4 exd4 5.exd4, play Nf3 and Nc3, castle, and use the open e-file.

why.text:
As Black, 3...c5 fights for the center at once. You accept a weak pawn in return for quick, active development.

rows: Rubinstein System: 4.cxd5 exd5, then Nf3, g3 and Bg2
The bishop on g2 hits d5, the isolated pawn. Castle and keep up the pressure.
Play ...Nc6 and ...Nf6. If White develops the f1 bishop before taking on d5, take on c4, then play ...a6, ...b5 and ...Bb7.
Develop with ...Nc6, ...Nf6 and ...Be7, and castle. Avoid needless trades.
Push ...d4! and win the pawn back later. Never 5...Bxc5?: 6.Qxd5 wins your d5 pawn.
Take the pawn with Qxd4 and keep it.

courses.repertoire: As White: Classical (5.Nf3, 6.Be2 and castling), with 9.b4 against the Mar del Plata. As Black: the Kazakh 6...Na6 against the Classical, and ...c5 against the Four Pawns and the Sämisch.
courses.summary: As White: develop naturally, castle, and let Black commit first. Close the center with d5 and race on the queenside with b4 and c5; against ...exd4, guard e4 with f3 and use your space. As Black: let White build the big center, castle behind the g7 bishop, then strike with ...e5 or ...c5. The Kazakh 6...Na6 and a knight on c5 keep the theory light against the Classical.
overview: As White: play the Classical: 5.Nf3, 6.Be2 and castle. You make no weakening pawn moves, so Black's attack has nothing to aim at until the center closes.

As White: after 6.Be2, Black's main reply is 6...e5, in about a third of those games, and 6...Nbd7 or 6...Nc6 usually lead to ...e5 as well. Castle first, then close the center with d5 or hold it with Be3.
As White: against 7...Nc6, the Mar del Plata, play 8.d5 and 9.b4. Your queenside attack with c5 must arrive before Black's ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5.
As White: against 7...exd4 8.Nxd4 Re8, guard e4 with 9.f3 at once. Natural moves such as 9.Bg5? or 9.Re1? let Black take on e4.
As White: against 6...c5, castle and take back on d4 with the knight. Your pawns on c4 and e4 form the Maroczy Bind, which clamps d5 and Black's freeing breaks.
As White: know the tricks: 5...e5?! 6.dxe5 wins a pawn before Black has castled, and the fork trick 8...Nxe4?? fails because your queen guards d4.
As Black: set up with ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6 and ...O-O, then strike at White's center with ...e5 or ...c5. Your king is safe behind the g7 bishop.

As Black: White's systems are spread out: 5.Nf3 comes up in about a sixth of your games, and the Four Pawns, the Sämisch, the Makogonov, 5.Be2 and 5.Bd3 in about 5 to 8% each. Learn the plan for each.
As Black: against the Classical, 6.Be2, play 6...Na6 and ...e5. When White closes the center with d5, put the knight on c5, play ...a5 so b4 can't chase it, then ...f5.
As Black: against the Four Pawns (5.f4) and the Sämisch (5.f3 and Be3), strike at once with ...c5. White's center is loose and the king is not castled yet.
As Black: against the Averbakh (Be2 and Bg5), play ...Na6 before ...e5. Otherwise Nd5 hits f6 and c7 and wins the exchange.
As Black: against 6.Bd3, play 6...Bg4 and pile up on d4 with ...Bxf3, ...Nc6 and ...Nd7. The natural Ne2?? then loses material to ...Nce5.

rows: The closed games: Black stakes a claim with a pawn on d5 at once, so White can no longer play e4 for free.
Black stops e4 with a piece instead of a pawn. The games range from solid (Queen's Indian) to sharp (King's Indian, Grünfeld).
A waiting move that usually transposes: after 2.c4 to the Queen's Gambit Declined (2...d5) or an Indian defense (2...Nf6); after 2.e4 to the French.

surveys.summary: 1.d4 usually leads to slower, more strategic games than 1.e4. Against 1...d5, White can skip the Queen's Gambit and play a system such as the London or the Colle: the same setup in almost every game, so they are easy to remember. The London is one of the most popular choices at club level (and works against 1...Nf6 too); the Colle is much rarer and is listed with the uncommon replies. surveys.subtitle: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4: the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Grünfeld, Queen's Indian and Benoni.

rows: Black lets White take the whole center, then hits it with ...e5 and attacks on the kingside. Sharp and double-edged.
The pin on c3 stops e4. Black is often ready to give up the bishop pair to double White's c-pawns.
Black invites a big white center with ...d5, then attacks it with the g7 bishop and ...c5.
Black gives a pawn for lasting pressure on the a- and b-files.
Black opens the e-file and pushes the queenside pawns, while White has more space in the center.
Black controls e4 and d5 from a distance with the queen's bishop on b7. Solid and positional.
Most transpose: 2...e6 with ...d5 becomes a Queen's Gambit Declined (about 10%). 2...e5 is the Budapest Gambit (9.5%, see Uncommon replies to 1.d4); 2...d6 is the Old Indian (4%).
table.note: Share: how often each defense comes up in games that reach 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. The King's Indian figure counts every 2...g6 game except the Grünfeld (3.Nc3 d5); the others are measured on the move order shown.

surveys.summary: Black develops the knight first and keeps the choice of setup open. The map shows where each defense starts; the table below it shows how often each one comes up.

surveys.name: Uncommon replies to 1.d4
surveys.subtitle: The Dutch Defense, the Budapest Gambit and White's Colle System, each played out to move 4.

rows: Black claims e4 with the f-pawn, for unbalanced play and kingside chances, at some cost to king safety.
A gambit: Black offers the e-pawn at once and usually wins it back with ...Ng4 and ...Nc6. Best as a surprise.
A quiet White system: d4, e3, Bd3 and Nbd2, then the break e4 opens lines toward Black's king.
table.note: Share: how often each opening comes up in games that start with 1.d4, in rated rapid and classical Lichess games between players averaging 1800 to 2199. The Dutch figure includes games that reach it by 1...e6 and a later ...f5. In the Colle, White chooses the opening; in the others, Black does.

surveys.name: Other first moves
surveys.subtitle: The five first moves you meet most besides 1.e4 and 1.d4, with Black's main replies, each played out to move 4.
surveys.summary: Each opening has one board and a Watch button for each of Black's main replies, played out to move 4 along the moves club players choose most often on Lichess. Under each board, White's plan and Black's plan are summed up in a few lines. No course is planned for these openings yet.

rows: White controls d5 from the side and often fianchettoes with g3 and Bg2. Positional games; after 1...e5 it is a Sicilian with colors reversed.
The most flexible first move: White develops, stops ...e5 and chooses a setup later. It usually turns into a 1.d4 opening, the English or the Réti.
White grabs e5 with the f-pawn: a Dutch Defense with colors reversed. Kingside attacking chances, at some cost to king safety.
White fianchettoes the queen's bishop toward e5 and plays against Black's center from the side. Offbeat, maneuvering games.
White fianchettoes the king's bishop and decides on the center later, often reaching a King's Indian Attack or an English. Slow and flexible.
